claims.quote: By 2021, the estimated cost of Cyber criminality is $6 trillion

check.reason: The deck's figure matches a widely cited Cybersecurity Ventures prediction, first published in 2016, of $6 trillion in annual cybercrime damages by 2021. It is a forecast from one research firm, and Ponemon's founder called it possibly too high.

sources.title: Cybersecurity Ventures
sources.quote: Cybersecurity Ventures predicts cybercrime damages will cost the world $6 trillion annually by 2021, up from $3 trillion in 2015.

sources.title: Dark Reading
sources.quote: While a $6 trillion estimate might be a little high, “a trillion dollars plus is a real possibility,” says Larry Ponemon, chairman and founder of the Ponemon Institute.

sources.title: Business Insurance
sources.quote: A report by U.S.-based cyber research firm Cybersecurity Ventures said that cybercrime will cost the world $6 trillion per year by 2021, up from $3 trillion in 2015, Cisomag reports.

claims.text: A hacker attack occurs every 39 seconds

check.reason: The 39-second figure is real, but it comes from a 2007 University of Maryland experiment on four deliberately weak Linux machines, so it is not a measured current global attack rate and the deck's wording overstates it.

sources.title: University of Maryland Clark School
sources.quote: The computers in our study were attacked, on average, 2,244 times a day.

sources.title: DeepStrike
sources.quote: At internet scale, malicious activity is effectively continuous, but there is no single defensible global "one attack every X seconds" rate for 2026.

sources.title: Dark Reading
sources.quote: A new University of Maryland study reports that the average computer on the Internet is attacked every 39 seconds.

claims.quote: The average cost of a data breach is $150 M.

check.reason: IBM's annual Cost of a Data Breach study puts the global average at about $4–5M, and even the US average is about $10–11.5M. That is far below the deck's $150M. The only figures near $150M are for mega-breaches of 50M+ records, which are not the average.

sources.title: IBM Think – What Is a Data Breach? (Cost of a Data Breach 2026)
sources.quote: According to IBM's Cost of a Data Breach 2026 report, the global average cost of a data breach is USD 4.99 million.

sources.title: IBM Think – 2025 Cost of a Data Breach Report
sources.quote: IBM's newly released 2025 Cost of a Data Breach Report found that average global costs dropped to USD 4.44 million—down from USD 4.88 million, or 9%, in the year prior.

sources.title: IBM Think – Cost of a data breach 2024: Financial industry
sources.quote: Both healthcare and finance saw the same costs for large-scale breaches: When 50 million records or more were compromised, average costs skyrocketed to USD 375 million.

questions.text: The deck says no competitor is crowd-based, open source or free, and that earlier attempts like Symantec and Talos missed the crowd approach. But fail2ban is free and open source, and AbuseIPDB and AlienVault OTX (since 2012) are crowd-sourced IP reputation services. Why are they not direct competitors, and what is your real differentiation and defensibility against them?
questions.why: Tests the contradicted 'no crowd-based/open/free competitor' claim, which underpins the 3.5% free-to-premium conversion target and the premium thesis.
questions.evidence_to_request: Competitive comparison against fail2ban, AbuseIPDB and AlienVault OTX (data coverage, report volume, API limits, pricing), plus any user migration or overlap data from beta users.

questions.text: You say thousands of machines already report attacks in real time, and that your database is the most accurate ever made. How many unique machines and reports per day are live today, and how have you measured accuracy or false positives against other reputation feeds?
questions.why: Tests the load-bearing traction and product claim (thousands of reporting machines, 'most accurate'), which supports adoption as the sole KPI and the €300K raise.
questions.evidence_to_request: Dashboard export of active agents and daily signals over time, a list of agent installs by geography, and any benchmark of false-positive/detection rates against other blocklists.

questions.text: You target a 3.5% free-to-premium conversion and plan premium sales and a Series A in March 2021. What benchmarks and funnel assumptions support 3.5%, and does 200K free API queries leave enough reason to upgrade?
questions.why: Tests the conversion assumption and free-tier design that drive the premium revenue case and the Series A timeline.
questions.evidence_to_request: Conversion model with assumptions (adoption, free-to-paid, ARPU), comparable open-core or freemium benchmarks, and free-tier usage data showing how many users approach the 200K query limit.

questions.text: You are raising about €300K with a team of 6, five of them on unemployment benefits, and a Series A planned for March 2021. What is the runway, what milestones does the round fund, and what adoption level must you hit to be Series A-ready?
questions.why: Tests the raise itself, which has no stated use of funds or runway, against a team largely on unemployment benefits and a single adoption KPI.
questions.evidence_to_request: Use-of-funds breakdown, 18-month budget and runway model, cap table with the team's €200K investment, and the adoption milestones targeted for the Series A.

questions.text: The deck says your previous company was sold in 2016 for 'tens of millions'. Public sources only confirm the NBS System sale to Oceanet, with about €6.7M in revenue. What was the actual price and what did each founder take home? Who among the trio has the 25 and 12 years of relevant security experience?
questions.why: Tests the team's credibility claim, which supports investor confidence in the €300K round and cannot be verified from public sources.
questions.evidence_to_request: Sale agreement summary or a founder proceeds statement, plus LinkedIn profiles or CVs for the three founders.
